beats.say: Imagine a modest monk in 608, suddenly thrust onto the papal throne after a sudden death.
He is Boniface IV, the first pope to convert the ancient Pantheon into a Christian shrine.
While Rome trembled, he ordered the Pantheon's massive bronze doors sealed, hiding pagan symbols from curious eyes.
Only months later, a fire in the basilica of St Peter forced him to salvage the sacred relics in a night.
He commissioned a stunning mosaic of the Virgin in the apse, a bold statement against lingering Arian art.
beats.visual: Mosaic of Virgin in apse early 7th century

beats.say: Boniface also granted the exiled bishop of Ravenna a tiny plot on the Aventine, sparking a property feud.
His most secret act: he quietly ordered the burial of a pagan philosopher's scrolls beneath the altar, fearing future heresy.
beats.visual: hidden scrolls beneath altar ancient church

beats.say: When he died in 615, the Vatican sealed his tomb, and the scrolls vanished, never to be catalogued.
beats.visual: Vatican tomb of Pope Boniface IV

beats.say: Centuries later, archaeologists uncovered a hidden niche in the Pantheon, confirming his covert burial of texts.
Thus Boniface IV reshaped Rome's sacred space, trading gold for secrecy, a move still echoing in Vatican archives.
